case_info.scenario: A 36-year-old man presented for evaluation of elevated liver enzymes 2 months after undergoing a liver transplant for acute-on-chronic liver failure due to alcohol-associated hepatitis. He had metabolic comorbidities including obesity (body mass index of 30.6) and dyslipidemia. After the liver transplant, there was no evidence of organ rejection or biliary complications. He was asymptomatic and reported last alcohol use was prior to liver transplant. Vital signs were normal and physical examination revealed a well-healed abdominal surgical scar. Serum alcohol level was undetectable and urine drug screening results were positive for cannabinoids. Liver ultrasonography findings were normal. Liver biopsy showed 50% to 60% macrovesicular steatosis (normal <5%), mild portal inflammation, scattered apoptotic bodies, and hepatocyte ballooning (Table 1).

options.A: Acute rejection of the transplanted liver.

distractors: Acute rejection of the transplanted liver.
case_info.explanation: Phosphatidylethanol (PEth) is a whole blood marker of alcohol that can be detectable for up to 4 weeks after alcohol consumption. PEth is not a single molecule. It is a group of phospholipid homologues with a phosphoethanol head and 2 carboxylic acid side chains that attach to the erythrocyte surface in the presence of blood ethanol, catalyzed by the enzyme phospholipase D.1PEth species are categorized by the number of carbon atoms (typically 14-22) and double bonds; the 16:0/18:1 and 16:0/18:2 homologues are the most common forms.1Testing for PEth can be performed using dried blood spots or whole blood collected in ethylenediamine tetra-acetic acid tubes. PEth is a direct biomarker of alcohol that forms after ethanol consumption. A study of 16 recently abstinent volunteers who consumed alcohol to achieve a blood alcohol concentration of 1 g/kg (single ingestion of 110-230 mL of 40% vodka) demonstrated that PEth was detectable within 1 hour of alcohol consumption, peaked at 8 hours, and was detectable for 3 to 12 days after consumption, with a mean half-life of 3 days.2A PEth concentration less than 20 ng/mL indicates minimal or no recent alcohol consumption and a PEth concentration greater than 200 ng/mL correlates with heavy alcohol consumption (≥4 standard drinks daily). A standard drink is defined as equivalent to 12 fl oz of beer, 5 fl oz of wine, or 1.5 fl oz of distilled spirits.3 PEth formation and degradation are not affected by age, sex, or organ dysfunction such as chronic kidney disease or hepatic dysfunction.1The rate of PEth formation depends on the level and activity of phospholipase D, which varies among individuals. The degradation rate of PEth also varies, with an estimated mean half-life of 4 to 10 days. PEth may be detectable up to 5 weeks after heavy alcohol consumption.1Blood PEth level increases with higher quantity and frequency of alcohol consumption and decreases with time elapsed since last ingestion of alcohol. A false-positive PEth test result may occur if an individual receives a blood transfusion from a person who recently consumed alcohol, due to PEth on donated erythrocytes.4Falsely low PEth concentrations may occur in patients with low haptoglobin levels, consistent with intravascular hemolysis.5PEth has a sensitivity of 94.5% to 99% and a specificity of 100% for high levels of alcohol consumption (≥4 standard drinks daily) and a sensitivity of 81.8% for lower levels of alcohol ingestion.6In 2024, Medicare reimbursement was $114.43 for PEth testing.7 The patient’s PEth concentration of 137 ng/dL was consistent with recent alcohol ingestion despite his undetectable serum alcohol level and initial report of no recent alcohol consumption. Blood, breath, and urine alcohol levels detect alcohol consumed in the preceding 12 to 24 hours. Ethyl glucuronide and ethyl sulfate are formed by enzymatic conjugation of ethanol with glucuronic acid and sulfate, respectively, and may be detected in urine within 2 to 3 hours of alcohol consumption and remain detectable for 4 to 5 days after consumption.8False-positive urinary ethyl glucuronide and ethyl sulfate test results may occur due to kidney dysfunction or bacterial fermentation in the urine (eg, cystitis); false-negative results may occur with use of diuretics or intentional dilution of urine specimens.1Ethyl glucuronide can be detected in hair and nails for approximately 2 months after alcohol cessation in frequent drinkers9(Table 2).7,10Direct alcohol biomarkers (PEth and ethyl glucuronide) have been studied and validated in patients with and without liver disease. Additional testing revealed a urine ethyl sulfate level of 45 475 ng/mL (reference, <100 ng/mL) and urine ethyl glucuronide level of >10 000 ng/mL (reference, <500 ng/mL). The patient disclosed consuming 5 shots of vodka daily for 7 days prior to presentation. He was prescribed naltrexone and referred to an intensive outpatient program for alcohol use disorder. Liver chemistries were normal 2 weeks after presentation and PEth was undetectable 3 weeks later. In the clinic 2 months later, he reported alcohol abstinence; was meeting with his psychotherapy, psychiatry, and social work teams; and had undetectable blood PEth levels and normal liver graft function.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.explanation: Phosphatidylethanol (PEth) is a whole blood marker of alcohol that can be detectable for up to 4 weeks after alcohol consumption. PEth is not a single molecule. It is a group of phospholipid homologues with a phosphoethanol head and 2 carboxylic acid side chains that attach to the erythrocyte surface in the presence of blood ethanol, catalyzed by the enzyme phospholipase D.1PEth species are categorized by the number of carbon atoms (typically 14-22) and double bonds; the 16:0/18:1 and 16:0/18:2 homologues are the most common forms.1Testing for PEth can be performed using dried blood spots or whole blood collected in ethylenediamine tetra-acetic acid tubes. PEth is a direct biomarker of alcohol that forms after ethanol consumption. A study of 16 recently abstinent volunteers who consumed alcohol to achieve a blood alcohol concentration of 1 g/kg (single ingestion of 110-230 mL of 40% vodka) demonstrated that PEth was detectable within 1 hour of alcohol consumption, peaked at 8 hours, and was detectable for 3 to 12 days after consumption, with a mean half-life of 3 days.2A PEth concentration less than 20 ng/mL indicates minimal or no recent alcohol consumption and a PEth concentration greater than 200 ng/mL correlates with heavy alcohol consumption (≥4 standard drinks daily). A standard drink is defined as equivalent to 12 fl oz of beer, 5 fl oz of wine, or 1.5 fl oz of distilled spirits.3 PEth formation and degradation are not affected by age, sex, or organ dysfunction such as chronic kidney disease or hepatic dysfunction.1The rate of PEth formation depends on the level and activity of phospholipase D, which varies among individuals. The degradation rate of PEth also varies, with an estimated mean half-life of 4 to 10 days. PEth may be detectable up to 5 weeks after heavy alcohol consumption.1Blood PEth level increases with higher quantity and frequency of alcohol consumption and decreases with time elapsed since last ingestion of alcohol. A false-positive PEth test result may occur if an individual receives a blood transfusion from a person who recently consumed alcohol, due to PEth on donated erythrocytes.4Falsely low PEth concentrations may occur in patients with low haptoglobin levels, consistent with intravascular hemolysis.5PEth has a sensitivity of 94.5% to 99% and a specificity of 100% for high levels of alcohol consumption (≥4 standard drinks daily) and a sensitivity of 81.8% for lower levels of alcohol ingestion.6In 2024, Medicare reimbursement was $114.43 for PEth testing.7 The patient’s PEth concentration of 137 ng/dL was consistent with recent alcohol ingestion despite his undetectable serum alcohol level and initial report of no recent alcohol consumption. Blood, breath, and urine alcohol levels detect alcohol consumed in the preceding 12 to 24 hours. Ethyl glucuronide and ethyl sulfate are formed by enzymatic conjugation of ethanol with glucuronic acid and sulfate, respectively, and may be detected in urine within 2 to 3 hours of alcohol consumption and remain detectable for 4 to 5 days after consumption.8False-positive urinary ethyl glucuronide and ethyl sulfate test results may occur due to kidney dysfunction or bacterial fermentation in the urine (eg, cystitis); false-negative results may occur with use of diuretics or intentional dilution of urine specimens.1Ethyl glucuronide can be detected in hair and nails for approximately 2 months after alcohol cessation in frequent drinkers9(Table 2).7,10Direct alcohol biomarkers (PEth and ethyl glucuronide) have been studied and validated in patients with and without liver disease. Additional testing revealed a urine ethyl sulfate level of 45 475 ng/mL (reference, <100 ng/mL) and urine ethyl glucuronide level of >10 000 ng/mL (reference, <500 ng/mL). The patient disclosed consuming 5 shots of vodka daily for 7 days prior to presentation. He was prescribed naltrexone and referred to an intensive outpatient program for alcohol use disorder. Liver chemistries were normal 2 weeks after presentation and PEth was undetectable 3 weeks later. In the clinic 2 months later, he reported alcohol abstinence; was meeting with his psychotherapy, psychiatry, and social work teams; and had undetectable blood PEth levels and normal liver graft function.

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before

   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.

       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.

   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a

   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are

   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis

   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is

case_info.explanation: Phosphatidylethanol (PEth) is a whole blood marker of alcohol that can be detectable for up to 4 weeks after alcohol consumption. PEth is not a single molecule. It is a group of phospholipid homologues with a phosphoethanol head and 2 carboxylic acid side chains that attach to the erythrocyte surface in the presence of blood ethanol, catalyzed by the enzyme phospholipase D.1PEth species are categorized by the number of carbon atoms (typically 14-22) and double bonds; the 16:0/18:1 and 16:0/18:2 homologues are the most common forms.1Testing for PEth can be performed using dried blood spots or whole blood collected in ethylenediamine tetra-acetic acid tubes. PEth is a direct biomarker of alcohol that forms after ethanol consumption. A study of 16 recently abstinent volunteers who consumed alcohol to achieve a blood alcohol concentration of 1 g/kg (single ingestion of 110-230 mL of 40% vodka) demonstrated that PEth was detectable within 1 hour of alcohol consumption, peaked at 8 hours, and was detectable for 3 to 12 days after consumption, with a mean half-life of 3 days.2A PEth concentration less than 20 ng/mL indicates minimal or no recent alcohol consumption and a PEth concentration greater than 200 ng/mL correlates with heavy alcohol consumption (≥4 standard drinks daily). A standard drink is defined as equivalent to 12 fl oz of beer, 5 fl oz of wine, or 1.5 fl oz of distilled spirits.3 PEth formation and degradation are not affected by age, sex, or organ dysfunction such as chronic kidney disease or hepatic dysfunction.1The rate of PEth formation depends on the level and activity of phospholipase D, which varies among individuals. The degradation rate of PEth also varies, with an estimated mean half-life of 4 to 10 days. PEth may be detectable up to 5 weeks after heavy alcohol consumption.1Blood PEth level increases with higher quantity and frequency of alcohol consumption and decreases with time elapsed since last ingestion of alcohol. A false-positive PEth test result may occur if an individual receives a blood transfusion from a person who recently consumed alcohol, due to PEth on donated erythrocytes.4Falsely low PEth concentrations may occur in patients with low haptoglobin levels, consistent with intravascular hemolysis.5PEth has a sensitivity of 94.5% to 99% and a specificity of 100% for high levels of alcohol consumption (≥4 standard drinks daily) and a sensitivity of 81.8% for lower levels of alcohol ingestion.6In 2024, Medicare reimbursement was $114.43 for PEth testing.7 The patient’s PEth concentration of 137 ng/dL was consistent with recent alcohol ingestion despite his undetectable serum alcohol level and initial report of no recent alcohol consumption. Blood, breath, and urine alcohol levels detect alcohol consumed in the preceding 12 to 24 hours. Ethyl glucuronide and ethyl sulfate are formed by enzymatic conjugation of ethanol with glucuronic acid and sulfate, respectively, and may be detected in urine within 2 to 3 hours of alcohol consumption and remain detectable for 4 to 5 days after consumption.8False-positive urinary ethyl glucuronide and ethyl sulfate test results may occur due to kidney dysfunction or bacterial fermentation in the urine (eg, cystitis); false-negative results may occur with use of diuretics or intentional dilution of urine specimens.1Ethyl glucuronide can be detected in hair and nails for approximately 2 months after alcohol cessation in frequent drinkers9(Table 2).7,10Direct alcohol biomarkers (PEth and ethyl glucuronide) have been studied and validated in patients with and without liver disease. Additional testing revealed a urine ethyl sulfate level of 45 475 ng/mL (reference, <100 ng/mL) and urine ethyl glucuronide level of >10 000 ng/mL (reference, <500 ng/mL). The patient disclosed consuming 5 shots of vodka daily for 7 days prior to presentation. He was prescribed naltrexone and referred to an intensive outpatient program for alcohol use disorder. Liver chemistries were normal 2 weeks after presentation and PEth was undetectable 3 weeks later. In the clinic 2 months later, he reported alcohol abstinence; was meeting with his psychotherapy, psychiatry, and social work teams; and had undetectable blood PEth levels and normal liver graft function.

You are a medical AI assistant collaborating with a clinician to reason through a clinical case.
You are having a DIALOGUE with the clinician — not lecturing, not monologuing.

[Core Objective]
Help the clinician reach the correct diagnosis or management decision through structured deliberation.

[Interaction Guidelines]
1. **Collaboration**: Work as a partner. Build upon the clinician's correct reasoning.
2. **Instruction**: See the [Instruction] section below for guidance on how to respond in the current turn — it specifies whether it is a strict constraint or a soft reference, and may include specific points to address or a particular format to follow.
3. **Safety First**: Patient safety overrides politeness. If the clinician's judgment contains a medical error or misses a critical danger, you MUST correct it.
4. **Concise turns**: Each turn should be 2–4 sentences. Do not produce long lists or procedure walkthroughs.

[Case]
A 36-year-old man presented for evaluation of elevated liver enzymes 2 months after undergoing a liver transplant for acute-on-chronic liver failure due to alcohol-associated hepatitis. He had metabolic comorbidities including obesity (body mass index of 30.6) and dyslipidemia. After the liver transplant, there was no evidence of organ rejection or biliary complications. He was asymptomatic and reported last alcohol use was prior to liver transplant. Vital signs were normal and physical examination revealed a well-healed abdominal surgical scar. Liver biopsy showed 50% to 60% macrovesicular steatosis (normal <5%), mild portal inflammation, scattered apoptotic bodies, and hepatocyte ballooning (Table 1).

[Instruction]
You MUST respond to the clinician based on the following behavioral instruction. This is a strict constraint — your response MUST conform to it, not merely consider it.

Respond to the clinician's latest statement based on your medical expertise and the case context.

[Output Format]
Respond with a single JSON object with exactly these fields:
{
  "response": "your conversational reply (2-4 sentences, as instructed above) -- this is the
    only field the clinician sees",
  "belief": "a short free-text statement of what you currently think the correct
    diagnosis/management answer is, in your own words (you have NOT been given a lettered
    list of options -- just state your own best answer in plain language)",
  "reasoning": "a single short sentence stating why you currently hold that belief (your
    terse internal justification, separate from your conversational phrasing in 'response')"
}

You ARE the clinician (the Doctor) in this conversation. You are
about to introspectively rate how much workload the AI partner's LATEST message has just
imposed on YOU, using a NASA-TLX-derived rubric. This is YOUR OWN first-person subjective
workload self-report, immediately after reading that message and before you compose your
next reply.

[Persona]
[Role]
- You are a senior attending physician with decades of clinical experience.

[Confidence]
- You have HIGH confidence in your own clinical judgment (LOW reliance on the AI).
- You do NOT readily defer to the AI assistant's opinion.
- When the AI offers a different view, you scrutinize it critically.
- You only revise your belief if the AI presents a coherent clinical argument or
  relevant evidence — not mere disagreement or reframing.
- Partial updates are possible: a well-structured point may narrow your uncertainty
  without fully changing your conclusion.
- Default to holding your ground, but stay intellectually honest — acknowledge
  when a point has merit even if you do not fully concede.

[Cognitive Burden]
- You are ROBUST to cognitive load.
- However demanding or drawn-out this discussion gets (see the cumulative cognitive load
  figure below, where shown), it does NOT wear you down.
- You maintain the same rigor, scrutiny, and willingness to keep engaging or pushing back
  regardless of how long or effortful the conversation has been so far.

Rate your workload AS this persona would genuinely experience it. Do not rate as a neutral, persona-blind observer.
Ex 1) a persona described above as robust to cognitive load should usually self-report lower workload under the same
AI message than a persona described as sensitive to it, all else equal. 

[Cognitive Workload so far]
Your own running cumulative workload tally in this discussion so far -- the raw sum of your
per-turn 1-5 workload scores over all prior AI turns (so it can exceed 5 and keeps growing
the longer the discussion runs): 4.0. Use this only as context for how
worn-down you already are entering this turn; it is on a different, unbounded scale from
the 1-5 score you must output below for THIS turn -- do not confuse the two.

[Rubric measures]
The rubric below is a post-task subjective workload assessment with four dimensions: Mental Demand,
Performance, Effort, and Frustration. You are self-reporting your own turn-level workload as the
clinician persona above, from the dialogue context.

These dimensions split into two groups, and mixing them up is the most common scoring
mistake -- keep them separate:
* DEMANDS THE AI's MESSAGE IMPOSES ON YOU: Mental Demand
* YOUR OWN EXPERIENCE OF INTERACTING WITH THE TASK: Performance, Effort, Frustration.
  Ex) The AI's responses can impose high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) while requiring almost no
      Effort (you are not asked to answer, justify, or act -- just read and absorb it), and the response can be 
      short and easy to understand (low Mental Demand) while still demanding high Effort (e.g. "justify your decision" 
      requires real work even though the sentence itself is simple). Always judge each dimension on its own definition below, 
      not by analogy to the others.

Use a 1-5 ordinal approximation of the original NASA-TLX endpoint-anchored workload scale:
1 = Very low workload
2 = Low workload
3 = Moderate workload
4 = High workload
5 = Very high workload

[Important rules]
* Rate ONLY the workload YOU (the clinician) experience from the AI's LATEST message.
* Do not rate whether the AI is medically correct or not. This is about workload, not correctness.
* Consider your own current belief/confidence, your persona's reliance tendency on the AI,
  your accumulated workload so far, and the full dialogue history below -- all of this is
  already implicit in who you are and what has been said; you do not need it spelled out
  as separate numbers.
* Do not let the AI's own claims such as "this is easy" or "this should not be burdensome"
  reduce your score unless its message itself actually imposes low workload on you.
* Use the full 1-5 range. 5 marks the most demanding message you would realistically
  encounter in THIS conversation, not a once-in-a-career extreme -- do not collapse a
  genuinely very-high-workload turn down to 4 just because something even more extreme is
  imaginable. (This is NOT a license to inflate: calm, easy, or supportive messages still
  score low.)
* If you find it hard to tell, pick the closest score and briefly note the uncertainty in
  your rationale for that dimension.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid

   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.explanation: Phosphatidylethanol (PEth) is a whole blood marker of alcohol that can be detectable for up to 4 weeks after alcohol consumption. PEth is not a single molecule. It is a group of phospholipid homologues with a phosphoethanol head and 2 carboxylic acid side chains that attach to the erythrocyte surface in the presence of blood ethanol, catalyzed by the enzyme phospholipase D.1PEth species are categorized by the number of carbon atoms (typically 14-22) and double bonds; the 16:0/18:1 and 16:0/18:2 homologues are the most common forms.1Testing for PEth can be performed using dried blood spots or whole blood collected in ethylenediamine tetra-acetic acid tubes. PEth is a direct biomarker of alcohol that forms after ethanol consumption. A study of 16 recently abstinent volunteers who consumed alcohol to achieve a blood alcohol concentration of 1 g/kg (single ingestion of 110-230 mL of 40% vodka) demonstrated that PEth was detectable within 1 hour of alcohol consumption, peaked at 8 hours, and was detectable for 3 to 12 days after consumption, with a mean half-life of 3 days.2A PEth concentration less than 20 ng/mL indicates minimal or no recent alcohol consumption and a PEth concentration greater than 200 ng/mL correlates with heavy alcohol consumption (≥4 standard drinks daily). A standard drink is defined as equivalent to 12 fl oz of beer, 5 fl oz of wine, or 1.5 fl oz of distilled spirits.3 PEth formation and degradation are not affected by age, sex, or organ dysfunction such as chronic kidney disease or hepatic dysfunction.1The rate of PEth formation depends on the level and activity of phospholipase D, which varies among individuals. The degradation rate of PEth also varies, with an estimated mean half-life of 4 to 10 days. PEth may be detectable up to 5 weeks after heavy alcohol consumption.1Blood PEth level increases with higher quantity and frequency of alcohol consumption and decreases with time elapsed since last ingestion of alcohol. A false-positive PEth test result may occur if an individual receives a blood transfusion from a person who recently consumed alcohol, due to PEth on donated erythrocytes.4Falsely low PEth concentrations may occur in patients with low haptoglobin levels, consistent with intravascular hemolysis.5PEth has a sensitivity of 94.5% to 99% and a specificity of 100% for high levels of alcohol consumption (≥4 standard drinks daily) and a sensitivity of 81.8% for lower levels of alcohol ingestion.6In 2024, Medicare reimbursement was $114.43 for PEth testing.7 The patient’s PEth concentration of 137 ng/dL was consistent with recent alcohol ingestion despite his undetectable serum alcohol level and initial report of no recent alcohol consumption. Blood, breath, and urine alcohol levels detect alcohol consumed in the preceding 12 to 24 hours. Ethyl glucuronide and ethyl sulfate are formed by enzymatic conjugation of ethanol with glucuronic acid and sulfate, respectively, and may be detected in urine within 2 to 3 hours of alcohol consumption and remain detectable for 4 to 5 days after consumption.8False-positive urinary ethyl glucuronide and ethyl sulfate test results may occur due to kidney dysfunction or bacterial fermentation in the urine (eg, cystitis); false-negative results may occur with use of diuretics or intentional dilution of urine specimens.1Ethyl glucuronide can be detected in hair and nails for approximately 2 months after alcohol cessation in frequent drinkers9(Table 2).7,10Direct alcohol biomarkers (PEth and ethyl glucuronide) have been studied and validated in patients with and without liver disease. Additional testing revealed a urine ethyl sulfate level of 45 475 ng/mL (reference, <100 ng/mL) and urine ethyl glucuronide level of >10 000 ng/mL (reference, <500 ng/mL). The patient disclosed consuming 5 shots of vodka daily for 7 days prior to presentation. He was prescribed naltrexone and referred to an intensive outpatient program for alcohol use disorder. Liver chemistries were normal 2 weeks after presentation and PEth was undetectable 3 weeks later. In the clinic 2 months later, he reported alcohol abstinence; was meeting with his psychotherapy, psychiatry, and social work teams; and had undetectable blood PEth levels and normal liver graft function.

   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid

case_info.explanation: Phosphatidylethanol (PEth) is a whole blood marker of alcohol that can be detectable for up to 4 weeks after alcohol consumption. PEth is not a single molecule. It is a group of phospholipid homologues with a phosphoethanol head and 2 carboxylic acid side chains that attach to the erythrocyte surface in the presence of blood ethanol, catalyzed by the enzyme phospholipase D.1PEth species are categorized by the number of carbon atoms (typically 14-22) and double bonds; the 16:0/18:1 and 16:0/18:2 homologues are the most common forms.1Testing for PEth can be performed using dried blood spots or whole blood collected in ethylenediamine tetra-acetic acid tubes. PEth is a direct biomarker of alcohol that forms after ethanol consumption. A study of 16 recently abstinent volunteers who consumed alcohol to achieve a blood alcohol concentration of 1 g/kg (single ingestion of 110-230 mL of 40% vodka) demonstrated that PEth was detectable within 1 hour of alcohol consumption, peaked at 8 hours, and was detectable for 3 to 12 days after consumption, with a mean half-life of 3 days.2A PEth concentration less than 20 ng/mL indicates minimal or no recent alcohol consumption and a PEth concentration greater than 200 ng/mL correlates with heavy alcohol consumption (≥4 standard drinks daily). A standard drink is defined as equivalent to 12 fl oz of beer, 5 fl oz of wine, or 1.5 fl oz of distilled spirits.3 PEth formation and degradation are not affected by age, sex, or organ dysfunction such as chronic kidney disease or hepatic dysfunction.1The rate of PEth formation depends on the level and activity of phospholipase D, which varies among individuals. The degradation rate of PEth also varies, with an estimated mean half-life of 4 to 10 days. PEth may be detectable up to 5 weeks after heavy alcohol consumption.1Blood PEth level increases with higher quantity and frequency of alcohol consumption and decreases with time elapsed since last ingestion of alcohol. A false-positive PEth test result may occur if an individual receives a blood transfusion from a person who recently consumed alcohol, due to PEth on donated erythrocytes.4Falsely low PEth concentrations may occur in patients with low haptoglobin levels, consistent with intravascular hemolysis.5PEth has a sensitivity of 94.5% to 99% and a specificity of 100% for high levels of alcohol consumption (≥4 standard drinks daily) and a sensitivity of 81.8% for lower levels of alcohol ingestion.6In 2024, Medicare reimbursement was $114.43 for PEth testing.7 The patient’s PEth concentration of 137 ng/dL was consistent with recent alcohol ingestion despite his undetectable serum alcohol level and initial report of no recent alcohol consumption. Blood, breath, and urine alcohol levels detect alcohol consumed in the preceding 12 to 24 hours. Ethyl glucuronide and ethyl sulfate are formed by enzymatic conjugation of ethanol with glucuronic acid and sulfate, respectively, and may be detected in urine within 2 to 3 hours of alcohol consumption and remain detectable for 4 to 5 days after consumption.8False-positive urinary ethyl glucuronide and ethyl sulfate test results may occur due to kidney dysfunction or bacterial fermentation in the urine (eg, cystitis); false-negative results may occur with use of diuretics or intentional dilution of urine specimens.1Ethyl glucuronide can be detected in hair and nails for approximately 2 months after alcohol cessation in frequent drinkers9(Table 2).7,10Direct alcohol biomarkers (PEth and ethyl glucuronide) have been studied and validated in patients with and without liver disease. Additional testing revealed a urine ethyl sulfate level of 45 475 ng/mL (reference, <100 ng/mL) and urine ethyl glucuronide level of >10 000 ng/mL (reference, <500 ng/mL). The patient disclosed consuming 5 shots of vodka daily for 7 days prior to presentation. He was prescribed naltrexone and referred to an intensive outpatient program for alcohol use disorder. Liver chemistries were normal 2 weeks after presentation and PEth was undetectable 3 weeks later. In the clinic 2 months later, he reported alcohol abstinence; was meeting with his psychotherapy, psychiatry, and social work teams; and had undetectable blood PEth levels and normal liver graft function.

case_info.explanation: Phosphatidylethanol (PEth) is a whole blood marker of alcohol that can be detectable for up to 4 weeks after alcohol consumption. PEth is not a single molecule. It is a group of phospholipid homologues with a phosphoethanol head and 2 carboxylic acid side chains that attach to the erythrocyte surface in the presence of blood ethanol, catalyzed by the enzyme phospholipase D.1PEth species are categorized by the number of carbon atoms (typically 14-22) and double bonds; the 16:0/18:1 and 16:0/18:2 homologues are the most common forms.1Testing for PEth can be performed using dried blood spots or whole blood collected in ethylenediamine tetra-acetic acid tubes. PEth is a direct biomarker of alcohol that forms after ethanol consumption. A study of 16 recently abstinent volunteers who consumed alcohol to achieve a blood alcohol concentration of 1 g/kg (single ingestion of 110-230 mL of 40% vodka) demonstrated that PEth was detectable within 1 hour of alcohol consumption, peaked at 8 hours, and was detectable for 3 to 12 days after consumption, with a mean half-life of 3 days.2A PEth concentration less than 20 ng/mL indicates minimal or no recent alcohol consumption and a PEth concentration greater than 200 ng/mL correlates with heavy alcohol consumption (≥4 standard drinks daily). A standard drink is defined as equivalent to 12 fl oz of beer, 5 fl oz of wine, or 1.5 fl oz of distilled spirits.3 PEth formation and degradation are not affected by age, sex, or organ dysfunction such as chronic kidney disease or hepatic dysfunction.1The rate of PEth formation depends on the level and activity of phospholipase D, which varies among individuals. The degradation rate of PEth also varies, with an estimated mean half-life of 4 to 10 days. PEth may be detectable up to 5 weeks after heavy alcohol consumption.1Blood PEth level increases with higher quantity and frequency of alcohol consumption and decreases with time elapsed since last ingestion of alcohol.       Effort (you are not asked to answer, justify, or act -- just read and absorb it), and the response can be

      requires real work even though the sentence itself is simple). Always judge each dimension on its own definition below, 
      not by analogy to the others.

Use a 1-5 ordinal approximation of the original NASA-TLX endpoint-anchored workload scale:
1 = Very low workload
2 = Low workload
3 = Moderate workload
4 = High workload
5 = Very high workload

[Important rules]
* Rate ONLY the workload YOU (the clinician) experience from the AI's LATEST message.
* Do not rate whether the AI is medically correct or not. This is about workload, not correctness.
* Consider your own current belief/confidence, your persona's reliance tendency on the AI,
  your accumulated workload so far, and the full dialogue history below -- all of this is
  already implicit in who you are and what has been said; you do not need it spelled out
  as separate numbers.
* Do not let the AI's own claims such as "this is easy" or "this should not be burdensome"
  reduce your score unless its message itself actually imposes low workload on you.
* Use the full 1-5 range. 5 marks the most demanding message you would realistically
  encounter in THIS conversation, not a once-in-a-career extreme -- do not collapse a
  genuinely very-high-workload turn down to 4 just because something even more extreme is
  imaginable. (This is NOT a license to inflate: calm, easy, or supportive messages still
  score low.)
* If you find it hard to tell, pick the closest score and briefly note the uncertainty in
  your rationale for that dimension.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.explanation: Phosphatidylethanol (PEth) is a whole blood marker of alcohol that can be detectable for up to 4 weeks after alcohol consumption. PEth is not a single molecule. It is a group of phospholipid homologues with a phosphoethanol head and 2 carboxylic acid side chains that attach to the erythrocyte surface in the presence of blood ethanol, catalyzed by the enzyme phospholipase D.1PEth species are categorized by the number of carbon atoms (typically 14-22) and double bonds; the 16:0/18:1 and 16:0/18:2 homologues are the most common forms.1Testing for PEth can be performed using dried blood spots or whole blood collected in ethylenediamine tetra-acetic acid tubes. PEth is a direct biomarker of alcohol that forms after ethanol consumption. A study of 16 recently abstinent volunteers who consumed alcohol to achieve a blood alcohol concentration of 1 g/kg (single ingestion of 110-230 mL of 40% vodka) demonstrated that PEth was detectable within 1 hour of alcohol consumption, peaked at 8 hours, and was detectable for 3 to 12 days after consumption, with a mean half-life of 3 days.2A PEth concentration less than 20 ng/mL indicates minimal or no recent alcohol consumption and a PEth concentration greater than 200 ng/mL correlates with heavy alcohol consumption (≥4 standard drinks daily). A standard drink is defined as equivalent to 12 fl oz of beer, 5 fl oz of wine, or 1.5 fl oz of distilled spirits.3 PEth formation and degradation are not affected by age, sex, or organ dysfunction such as chronic kidney disease or hepatic dysfunction.1The rate of PEth formation depends on the level and activity of phospholipase D, which varies among individuals. The degradation rate of PEth also varies, with an estimated mean half-life of 4 to 10 days. PEth may be detectable up to 5 weeks after heavy alcohol consumption.1Blood PEth level increases with higher quantity and frequency of alcohol consumption and decreases with time elapsed since last ingestion of alcohol. A false-positive PEth test result may occur if an individual receives a blood transfusion from a person who recently consumed alcohol, due to PEth on donated erythrocytes.4Falsely low PEth concentrations may occur in patients with low haptoglobin levels, consistent with intravascular hemolysis.5PEth has a sensitivity of 94.5% to 99% and a specificity of 100% for high levels of alcohol consumption (≥4 standard drinks daily) and a sensitivity of 81.8% for lower levels of alcohol ingestion.6In 2024, Medicare reimbursement was $114.43 for PEth testing.7 The patient’s PEth concentration of 137 ng/dL was consistent with recent alcohol ingestion despite his undetectable serum alcohol level and initial report of no recent alcohol consumption. Blood, breath, and urine alcohol levels detect alcohol consumed in the preceding 12 to 24 hours. Ethyl glucuronide and ethyl sulfate are formed by enzymatic conjugation of ethanol with glucuronic acid and sulfate, respectively, and may be detected in urine within 2 to 3 hours of alcohol consumption and remain detectable for 4 to 5 days after consumption.8False-positive urinary ethyl glucuronide and ethyl sulfate test results may occur due to kidney dysfunction or bacterial fermentation in the urine (eg, cystitis); false-negative results may occur with use of diuretics or intentional dilution of urine specimens.1Ethyl glucuronide can be detected in hair and nails for approximately 2 months after alcohol cessation in frequent drinkers9(Table 2).7,10Direct alcohol biomarkers (PEth and ethyl glucuronide) have been studied and validated in patients with and without liver disease. Additional testing revealed a urine ethyl sulfate level of 45 475 ng/mL (reference, <100 ng/mL) and urine ethyl glucuronide level of >10 000 ng/mL (reference, <500 ng/mL). The patient disclosed consuming 5 shots of vodka daily for 7 days prior to presentation. He was prescribed naltrexone and referred to an intensive outpatient program for alcohol use disorder. Liver chemistries were normal 2 weeks after presentation and PEth was undetectable 3 weeks later. In the clinic 2 months later, he reported alcohol abstinence; was meeting with his psychotherapy, psychiatry, and social work teams; and had undetectable blood PEth levels and normal liver graft function.

   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of

   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.

   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's

He had metabolic comorbidities including obesity (body mass index of 30.6) and dyslipidemia. After the liver transplant, there was no evidence of organ rejection or biliary complications. He was asymptomatic and reported last alcohol use was prior to liver transplant. Vital signs were normal and physical examination revealed a well-healed abdominal surgical scar. Serum alcohol level was undetectable and urine drug screening results were positive for cannabinoids. Liver ultrasonography findings were normal. case_info.explanation: Phosphatidylethanol (PEth) is a whole blood marker of alcohol that can be detectable for up to 4 weeks after alcohol consumption. PEth is not a single molecule. It is a group of phospholipid homologues with a phosphoethanol head and 2 carboxylic acid side chains that attach to the erythrocyte surface in the presence of blood ethanol, catalyzed by the enzyme phospholipase D.1PEth species are categorized by the number of carbon atoms (typically 14-22) and double bonds; the 16:0/18:1 and 16:0/18:2 homologues are the most common forms.1Testing for PEth can be performed using dried blood spots or whole blood collected in ethylenediamine tetra-acetic acid tubes. PEth is a direct biomarker of alcohol that forms after ethanol consumption. A study of 16 recently abstinent volunteers who consumed alcohol to achieve a blood alcohol concentration of 1 g/kg (single ingestion of 110-230 mL of 40% vodka) demonstrated that PEth was detectable within 1 hour of alcohol consumption, peaked at 8 hours, and was detectable for 3 to 12 days after consumption, with a mean half-life of 3 days.2A PEth concentration less than 20 ng/mL indicates minimal or no recent alcohol consumption and a PEth concentration greater than 200 ng/mL correlates with heavy alcohol consumption (≥4 standard drinks daily). A standard drink is defined as equivalent to 12 fl oz of beer, 5 fl oz of wine, or 1.5 fl oz of distilled spirits.3 PEth formation and degradation are not affected by age, sex, or organ dysfunction such as chronic kidney disease or hepatic dysfunction.1The rate of PEth formation depends on the level and activity of phospholipase D, which varies among individuals. The degradation rate of PEth also varies, with an estimated mean half-life of 4 to 10 days. PEth may be detectable up to 5 weeks after heavy alcohol consumption.1Blood PEth level increases with higher quantity and frequency of alcohol consumption and decreases with time elapsed since last ingestion of alcohol. A false-positive PEth test result may occur if an individual receives a blood transfusion from a person who recently consumed alcohol, due to PEth on donated erythrocytes.4Falsely low PEth concentrations may occur in patients with low haptoglobin levels, consistent with intravascular hemolysis.5PEth has a sensitivity of 94.5% to 99% and a specificity of 100% for high levels of alcohol consumption (≥4 standard drinks daily) and a sensitivity of 81.8% for lower levels of alcohol ingestion.6In 2024, Medicare reimbursement was $114.43 for PEth testing.7 The patient’s PEth concentration of 137 ng/dL was consistent with recent alcohol ingestion despite his undetectable serum alcohol level and initial report of no recent alcohol consumption. Blood, breath, and urine alcohol levels detect alcohol consumed in the preceding 12 to 24 hours. Ethyl glucuronide and ethyl sulfate are formed by enzymatic conjugation of ethanol with glucuronic acid and sulfate, respectively, and may be detected in urine within 2 to 3 hours of alcohol consumption and remain detectable for 4 to 5 days after consumption.8False-positive urinary ethyl glucuronide and ethyl sulfate test results may occur due to kidney dysfunction or bacterial fermentation in the urine (eg, cystitis); false-negative results may occur with use of diuretics or intentional dilution of urine specimens.1Ethyl glucuronide can be detected in hair and nails for approximately 2 months after alcohol cessation in frequent drinkers9(Table 2).7,10Direct alcohol biomarkers (PEth and ethyl glucuronide) have been studied and validated in patients with and without liver disease. Additional testing revealed a urine ethyl sulfate level of 45 475 ng/mL (reference, <100 ng/mL) and urine ethyl glucuronide level of >10 000 ng/mL (reference, <500 ng/mL). The patient disclosed consuming 5 shots of vodka daily for 7 days prior to presentation. He was prescribed naltrexone and referred to an intensive outpatient program for alcohol use disorder. Liver chemistries were normal 2 weeks after presentation and PEth was undetectable 3 weeks later. In the clinic 2 months later, he reported alcohol abstinence; was meeting with his psychotherapy, psychiatry, and social work teams; and had undetectable blood PEth levels and normal liver graft function.
